title: Navratri: the nine nights and what each one is about | Ask Tota
description: Nine nights, nine forms of Durga, one tithi-based calendar. Here is what each night marks, why the dates move, and why the colour list is newer than you think.
og_title: The nine nights, and what each one is actually about
og_description: Nine forms, in a fixed order, set by tithi and not by the calendar. Plus the honest note about where the colour chart came from.
h1: nine nights, nine forms, one moving date
dek: sharad navratri runs from the first tithi of the bright fortnight of ashwin. here is what each of the nine nights marks, why there are actually four navratris a year, and the honest story behind the colour chart everyone shares.

faq.q: what are the nine forms of durga?
faq.a: shailaputri, brahmacharini, chandraghanta, kushmanda, skandamata, katyayani, kalaratri, mahagauri and siddhidatri. together they are the navadurga, and the order is fixed.

faq.q: why do navratri dates change every year?
faq.a: because it is set by tithi, not by the solar calendar. sharad navratri begins on the first tithi of the bright fortnight of ashwin, and a lunar month is about 29.5 days, so it drifts against the gregorian calendar.

faq.q: how many navratris are there in a year?
faq.a: four. chaitra navratri in spring and sharad navratri in autumn are the widely observed ones. two more, in magha and ashadha, are called gupt navratri and are kept much more quietly.

faq.q: why is navratri sometimes eight days?
faq.a: tithi kshaya. a tithi can begin and end without ever being current at sunrise, so it drops out of the calendar and the festival runs a day short. it is a calendar artefact, not an omission.
the establishing of the pot on the first day, which formally opens the observance. it has its own muhurat, usually in the first third of the day, and it is avoided during specific periods.

the nine colour list is a modern convention, popularised through newspapers in western india over the last few decades. it is genuinely enjoyable and it is not classical, and both of those things can be true.

faq.q: what is the difference between navratri and durga puja?
faq.a: they are the same season observed differently. durga puja in bengal concentrates on the last few days, with the idol installed on shashthi and immersed on dashami.

faq.q: what happens on the tenth day?
faq.a: dashami, which is dussehra or vijayadashami. it closes the nine nights and is treated as one of the most auspicious days of the year for beginnings.

faq.q: does navratri have anything to do with the grahas?
faq.a: not directly. the timing is lunar and tithi-based, so it is calendar astronomy rather than a planetary reading. the observance itself is devotional, not astrological.

faq.q: why does the fasting differ between families?
faq.a: because the rules are regional and always have been. what counts as permitted food, whether grains are avoided, and how many days are kept vary by community and by household.

faq.q: what is the story behind the nine nights?
faq.a: the widely told version is the battle between durga and mahishasura, concluding in victory on the tenth day. the specifics vary by region, and several traditions attach different narratives to the same nine nights.
sharad navratri, in the autumn. it leads into dussehra and then into diwali about twenty days later, which makes it the opening of the busiest stretch of the indian festival calendar.
